title: Exposure to grass pollen--but not birch pollen--affects lung function in Swedish children.
ehr_evidence: Children belonging to the Swedish birth cohort BAMSE underwent clinical examination including lung-function testing and blood sampling for measuring serum immunoglobulin E (IgE) against common airborne and food allergens (ImmunoCAP System; Phadia AB, Uppsala, Sweden) at eight (N = 1838) and sixteen years of age (N = 2063).
summary: In the Swedish BAMSE birth cohort, daily pollen and air pollution concentrations were associated with reduced FEV1 in 8-year-old children exposed to grass pollen, with stronger effects among pollen-sensitized children.
key_findings: Grass pollen exposure the day before lung-function testing was associated with reduced FEV1 in 8-year-olds (-32.4 ml; 95% CI: -50.6 to -14.2, for an increase in three pollen counts/m³).
The negative effect of grass pollen on lung function was stronger in children sensitized to different pollen allergens (FEV1; -41.6 ml; 95% CI: -68.3 to -14.8).
An interaction between grass pollen exposure and sensitization to pollen allergens was detected (P = 0.05 and 0.01 for FEV1 and FVC, respectively).
No associations were found for birch or other pollen exposure in the 8-year-olds.
Pollen exposure was not related to lung function in the 16-year-olds.
captured_features: daily pollen counts for nine pollen types
population: Swedish children from the BAMSE birth cohort living in the Stockholm region, aged 8 (N = 1838) and 16 (N = 2063) years.
exposure_domain: Pollen/allergen exposure (grass, birch, and other pollen) with air pollution
limitations: Lung-function measurements were not performed during the summer, so it is not possible to judge whether effects relate to acute exposure or longer-term exposure.
No data on serum-specific IgG and IgG4 against pollen to evaluate tolerance development.
Pollen concentrations in 2003 and 2004 were relatively low for both birch and grass.
Observational design with potential residual confounding.
